context.text: The Church of Alexandria came out of the Great Persecution with its bishop Peter a martyr and its people divided. Achillas succeeded Peter for a short time, and then Alexander, a gentle and learned man, became bishop of the city, the greatest see of the East. Among his presbyters was Arius, priest of the church of Baucalis by the harbour, a Libyan by birth, ascetic, able in argument and much admired.

Socrates tells how the quarrel began. Alexander, teaching his clergy one day on the unity of the Holy Trinity, spoke of it with some philosophical subtlety. Arius thought he heard in it the old error of Sabellius, who confused the Father and the Son, and went to the opposite extreme:

'If,' said he, 'the Father begot the Son, he that was begotten had a beginning of existence: and from this it is evident, that there was a time when the Son was not. It therefore necessarily follows, that he had his substance from nothing.'
context.source: Socrates, Church History I.5, tr. A. C. Zenos (NPNF2 vol. 2, 1890)

narrative.text: Arius taught this openly and found followers among the clergy, the virgins and the people of Alexandria; his supporters later said he put his teaching into songs that sailors and millers could sing. Socrates writes that from a little spark a large fire was kindled:
for the evil which began in the Church at Alexandria, ran throughout all Egypt, Libya, and the upper Thebes, and at length diffused itself over the rest of the provinces and cities.
narrative.source: Socrates, Church History I.6, tr. A. C. Zenos (NPNF2 vol. 2, 1890)

narrative.text: Alexander first tried to reason with him, then gathered a council of the bishops of Egypt and Libya, which excommunicated Arius and those who held with him. Alexander wrote to the bishops of the whole Church to warn them, setting out what the new teachers said:
That God was not always the Father, but that there was a period when he was not the Father; that the Word of God was not from eternity, but was made out of nothing
narrative.source: St Alexander of Alexandria, Encyclical Letter, in Socrates, Church History I.6 (NPNF2 vol. 2, 1890)

narrative.text: Arius left Egypt and looked for friends abroad. He found the most powerful in Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, the eastern capital, who had studied as he had under Lucian of Antioch. To him Arius wrote, complaining that his bishop had driven him from the city:
We are persecuted, because we say that the Son has a beginning, but that God is without beginning.
narrative.source: Arius, Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret, Church History I.4, tr. B. Jackson (NPNF2 vol. 3, 1892)

narrative.text: Letters flew between the churches; councils met on each side; the dispute was argued in the streets and mocked in the theatres. When Constantine became master of the East in 324 he was grieved to find the Church divided, and sent Hosius of Cordova to Alexandria with a letter to Alexander and Arius, urging them to make peace over what he took to be a question of words. It was not, and the letter failed. The emperor then called a council of the whole Church, to meet at Nicaea in 325.

significance.text: The question Arius raised went to the heart of the faith: whether the Son who became man for us is God, or the highest of God's creatures. If He is a creature, a creature saves us, and the worship Christians had always given to Christ is idolatry. The Church's answer, given at Nicaea and defended for half a century by St Athanasius, Alexander's young deacon, was that the Son is of one essence with the Father, eternally begotten, true God from true God. The Creed the faithful sing at every Liturgy was shaped by this controversy.

consequences.text: The quarrel did not end at Nicaea. Through Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party the Arians won the favour of later emperors, and the struggle went on until the Second Ecumenical Council in 381. The Church keeps St Alexander's memory on 29 May.

uncertainty: The date is not certain: the quarrel is usually placed between 318 and 321, and the order of the first councils and letters is disputed. The account of how it began comes from historians writing a century later, who did not agree on every detail; Sozomen, for instance, says Alexander at first heard both sides patiently. The songs of Arius's Thalia are known only from quotations by his opponents.

people.name: Arius
people.role: Presbyter of Baucalis in Alexandria, who taught that the Son had a beginning and was made from nothing.

people.name: St Alexander of Alexandria
people.role: Bishop of Alexandria, who excommunicated Arius and warned the whole Church against his teaching.

people.name: St Athanasius the Great
people.role: Alexander's deacon and secretary, later his successor and the champion of Nicaea.

people.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
people.role: Bishop of the eastern capital, Arius's most powerful supporter.

people.name: St Constantine the Great
people.role: Emperor, who tried to reconcile the parties and then called the Council of Nicaea.

people.name: Hosius of Cordova
people.role: Bishop and counsellor of Constantine, sent to Alexandria with the emperor's letter.
